q: The official reason given by the British government for the partition of Bengal (announced in December 1903) was:
o: That Bengal, with a population of about 78 million, had become too big to be administered efficiently
That Calcutta could no longer serve as a capital
That Bengal's Muslims demanded a separate province
That Bengal wanted to be divided into linguistic zones

q: The partition of Bengal was designed to divide the Bengali people along which two lines, according to the chapter's analysis?
o: Caste and class
Coastal and inland regions
Language (reducing Bengalis to a minority in the new Bengal province) and religion (creating a Hindu-majority west and Muslim-majority east)
Urban and rural population

q: The formal proclamation of the Swadeshi Movement, including the passage of the Boycott Resolution, was made at a massive meeting held at:
o: Nagpur in 1907
Surat in December 1907
Benaras in December 1905
Calcutta Townhall on August 7, 1905

q: October 16, 1905, the day the partition of Bengal formally came into force, was observed throughout Bengal as:
o: A public holiday declared by the government
A day of celebration with fireworks
The founding day of the Indian National Congress
A day of mourning, marked by fasting, bathing in the Ganga and singing Bande Mataram in processions

q: Which of the following is identified as one of the three key reasons for the Extremists gaining dominant influence over the Swadeshi Movement in Bengal after 1905?
o: The Moderate-led movement had failed to yield results, and government repression had embittered the nationalists
The Muslim League fully supported the Extremist programme
The British government officially endorsed Extremist leadership
The Moderates voluntarily handed over leadership to the Extremists

q: Aurobindo Ghosh described the purpose of the Extremist programme of passive resistance as aiming to:
o: "Make the administration under present conditions impossible by an organised refusal to do anything which will help either the British commerce or British officialdom"
Organise an armed uprising against British garrisons
Establish a parallel government in exile
Persuade the British Parliament to grant dominion status immediately

q: The All India Muslim League was founded on December 30, 1905 (some sources say 1906), with support from which loyalist figure who backed the partition of Bengal?
o: Nawab Salimullah of Dacca
Sir Syed Ahmed Khan
Maulana Azad
Aga Khan

q: Which of the following is identified as a reason for the decline of the Swadeshi Movement by 1908?
o: Severe government repression, lack of an effective organisational structure, and the movement's narrow social base confined largely to upper and middle classes
Total absence of any government repression
Universal support across all religious communities, making further mobilisation unnecessary
Complete success in achieving all its demands

q: Despite its decline, the Swadeshi Movement is regarded as a 'turning point' in Indian nationalism mainly because:
o: It drew in previously untouched sections like students, women and workers, and generated ideas and techniques (passive resistance, non-cooperation) later used in Gandhian politics
It led immediately to full independence for India
It ended the Moderate-Extremist divide within the Congress
It resulted in universal adult franchise being granted

q: According to the chapter's comparison of Moderates and Extremists, the Moderates' ideological inspiration was drawn mainly from:
o: Western liberal thought and European history
Marxist class analysis
Islamic reformist thought
Indian history and Hindu traditional symbols

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the Extremists' view from the Moderates' regarding political connections with Britain?
o: Neither group had any clear position on this issue
Both groups agreed that British connections were harmful to India
The Extremists believed such connections would perpetuate British exploitation, while the Moderates believed connections with Britain served India's interests
The Extremists supported closer ties with Britain, while the Moderates opposed any connection

q: Which of the following is identified as a negative or 'socially reactionary' aspect of the Extremist ideology despite its politically progressive stance on mass mobilisation?
o: Revivalist and obscurantist undertones, such as Tilak's opposition to the Age of Consent Bill and use of Hindu festivals, which alienated many Muslims
Full support for women's rights and gender equality reforms
Complete rejection of any religious symbolism in politics
Active collaboration with the British government on all policy matters

q: At the Surat session (1907), the Moderates opposed Tilak's presidency partly on the ground that:
o: Tilak supported the partition of Bengal
A leader from the host province (Tilak from Bombay, where Surat is located) could not be session president
Tilak had never been a Congress member
Tilak was too moderate for the Extremist camp

q: Bal Gangadhar Tilak was tried for sedition in 1909 for articles he wrote in Kesari regarding:
o: A bomb thrown by Bengal revolutionaries at Muzaffarpur, which killed two European women
The formation of the Muslim League
The Ilbert Bill controversy
The partition of Bengal

q: John Morley, the Secretary of State for India, described the British government's strategy towards nationalists during this phase using which policy metaphor?
o: 'Scorched earth' — total suppression with no concessions
'Carrot and stick' — a three-pronged approach of repression, conciliation and further suppression
'Salami slicing' — gradual territorial annexation
'Divide and conquer' — encouraging Hindu-Muslim conflict exclusively

q: The Simla Deputation of October 1906, led by the Aga Khan, met Lord Minto to demand:
o: A separate Muslim province carved out of Punjab
Separate electorates for Muslims and representation in excess of their numerical strength
Abolition of the zamindari system in Bengal
Reservation for Muslims in the Indian Civil Service examination alone

q: Regarding the budget provisions under the Indian Councils Act of 1909, legislatures were permitted to:
o: Reject the budget entirely if a majority so wished
Vote on separate items of the budget, though the budget as a whole could not be voted upon
Have no role whatsoever in budget matters
Vote upon and amend the entire budget freely

q: Lord Morley's statement — "If it could be said that this chapter of reforms led directly or indirectly to the establishment of a parliamentary system in India, I, for one, would have nothing at all to do with it" — reveals that the Morley-Minto Reforms:
o: Were explicitly designed to grant full self-government
Aimed to abolish the office of viceroy
Were meant to immediately end separate electorates
Were never intended to lead towards responsible, parliamentary self-government for India

q: Jawaharlal Nehru's critique of the separate electorates introduced by the Morley-Minto Reforms described their effect as:
o: Strengthening national unity across communities
Having a negligible long-term political impact
Creating a political barrier that grew with every extension of franchise, corrupting the entire political and social system 'like some canker'
Improving administrative efficiency without social cost
